title: The Job
short: The party meets their contact by description, receives the sealed package, asks questions, and agrees to roll out.
long: A real conversation at the edge of the city. The whole crew, including Marlowe or a chosen replacement PC for Keystone custody, receives the job together. Sabine Quillon can appear here as the optional backup NPC job-giver if the table should not put that role on the Marlowe player.
read: The crew gathers at the carriage as the sealed crate waits inside, stamped with enough authorization marks to make opening it feel expensive.
gm: Do not play Emeris Crown Holdings as the villain yet. They are the employer and the system. Let suspicion emerge slowly.
prompt: Fantasy corporate delivery briefing at dawn: a courier crew gathers beside a sealed glowing crate loaded into a carriage; five adventurers prepare gear; subtle corporate seals and permits; no monsters, no strixwolf, no undead.
arc_role: Contract orientation, played briefing, and threshold transition
caption: Played briefing scene: description first, names through dialogue.
image_alt: The Job scene art for Act 0 - The Contract.
image_prompt_used: Fantasy corporate delivery briefing at dawn: a courier crew gathers beside a sealed glowing crate loaded into a carriage; five adventurers prepare gear; subtle corporate seals and permits; no monsters, no strixwolf, no undead. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: A professional but slightly ominous delivery briefing. The crate is heavy, sealed, and important, but the full truth is withheld. The party starts inside the system rather than against it. Run this scene as contract / ordinary frame: The party begins inside the system: hired, trusted, and carrying more risk than they know. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: At the edge of the warded road, a woman waits beside a loaded carriage. She looks like your contact for this job, but she has not introduced herself yet.
gm_notes: Do not play Emeris Crown Holdings as the villain yet. They are the employer and the system. Let suspicion emerge slowly.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
[ADD/GUARANTEED] Grail-branded bounty board: "STRIXWOLF: APEX FOREST HAZARD. Sightings up 300%. Bounty payable in Marks."
[ADD/GUARANTEED] Couriers or a clerk trade fearful route gossip: the Preserve "takes one a week now."
[ADD/EARNED] A player asking what they know receives the corporate line: strixwolves are vicious pack predators. (Knowledge Easy 10)

crate hinges humming under the morning noise

If Sabine is used, she keeps her voice even but checks the seal twice
Garrick watches the exits by habit
Varian tracks the road before anyone asks

Loreborne: spots older legal, heraldic, or ward-craft language under the branding.
Underborne: notices service doors, hidden routes, and who built the thing nobody credits.
Highborne: reads etiquette, class panic, and reputational risk.
Ridgeborne: notices stonework, weight, pressure, and structural weakness.

public_objective: Meet the contact, take custody of the sealed package, ask what you need to ask, and decide to roll out.
gm_script: At the edge of the warded road, a woman waits beside a loaded carriage. She has a book, a folded route-map, and the posture of someone trying not to look nervous. She looks across the group and says, 'You're the crew? Good. We're losing daylight.' What do you do?
player_takeaway: I can ask practical questions and learn names through play.
story_takeaway: The job becomes concrete: contact, carriage, package, destination, pay, and unease.
mechanic_takeaway: Optional social/reading rolls can reveal nervousness or corporate framing, but the scene works without dice.
gm_checklist: If using Sabine, show the contact image before saying her name.
Show the package image only as a sealed crate.
Ask 'Any questions before you roll out?' before moving to the threshold.
gm_private: Correction reminder: Marlowe stays a PC and the package custodian in the group unless Kyle chooses a replacement PC for package custody.
Sabine is optional backup job-giver only for S00-01. Use her when you do not want the Marlowe player to carry the table-facing job-giver role.
Everyone receives the job together, including Marlowe or the chosen replacement PC for package custody.
Marlowe's player gets her per-character job-scene benefit: bonus insight and an extra Arcana check at The Job.
Sabine may not know the full contents either if she is used; do not over-explain the package.
Sabine only needs to be in play for this Prologue job briefing and questions. After the handoff, the crew owns the route.
The manufactured-danger truth should feel like a faint mismatch, not a reveal.
gm_examples: If using Sabine and a PC asks her name: 'Sabine. Sabine Quillon. You're the crew Emeris sent? Good. We're losing daylight.'
If a PC asks what's inside: 'Above your pay grade and mine. Sealed means sealed.'
If the table stalls: 'She's waiting. Anyone have a question before the carriage rolls?'

player_beats.label: Meet the contact
player_beats.title: Your Contact
player_beats.alt: A finely dressed woman with a book and route map waits beside a carriage.
player_beats.caption: A finely dressed woman with a book, a creased route-map, and a fighter's wariness waits beside a loaded carriage.
player_beats.player_text: At the warded road, a sleep-frayed woman waits beside a loaded carriage: good boots, worn coat, a book, creased route-map, and the posture of someone expecting trouble. She looks you over. What do you do?
player_beats.gm_script: Use this beat for Sabine only if you want the optional backup NPC job-giver. If Sabine is in play, do not say her name until the players ask or she introduces herself. Push her image to the player display here. Marlowe remains a PC custodian in the crew and receives the job with everyone else.
player_beats.story_takeaway: The contact is a real, frayed person, not just a corporate mouthpiece.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Model the core loop: ask a question, get an answer.
player_beats.player_takeaway: The woman has a name once I engage with her.

player.title: Engagement reveals the contact
player.statement: The contact has a name when players ask or she introduces herself.
player.body: If Marlowe is a PC, do not make Marlowe the briefer. Marlowe receives the job with everyone else and can still carry custodian pressure.
player.say: "A tired, well-dressed field agent watches the crew from beside the carriage. She looks ready to talk, but she has not volunteered much yet."
player.ask: If players ask her name: "Sabine. Sabine Quillon. You are the crew Emeris sent? Good. We are losing daylight."
player.deeper: If Marlowe is a PC, do not make Marlowe the briefer. Marlowe receives the job with everyone else and can still carry custodian pressure.

story.title: The contact is nervous but capable
story.statement: The contact's tension gives the company story a human crack.
story.body: Do not reveal manufactured danger here. The useful clue is emotional: competence plus nerves.
story.say: "She is not falling apart. She is competent, tired, and watching the road like it has disappointed her before."
story.ask: If players ask whether she is lying: "On Instinct or Presence 13, she is not simply lying; she is repeating a company-safe version of danger while worrying about the parts she cannot control."
story.deeper: Do not reveal manufactured danger here. The useful clue is emotional: competence plus nerves.

mechanic.title: Social reads follow player approach
mechanic.statement: Reading the contact uses Instinct; pressing or reassuring her uses Presence.
mechanic.body: On Fear, give the truth with pressure: she notices the read, gets guarded, or hurries the handoff.
mechanic.say: "If you watch her tells, roll Instinct. If you press, charm, or reassure her, roll Presence. Difficulty 13 either way."
mechanic.ask: If players ask what success gives: "You learn she is scared of the run, not of you, and that the official danger line sounds practiced."
mechanic.deeper: On Fear, give the truth with pressure: she notices the read, gets guarded, or hurries the handoff.

player_beats.label: Briefing
player_beats.title: The Sealed Package
player_beats.alt: A sealed cargo crate in a carriage.
player_beats.caption: A sealed crate sits in the back of the carriage.
player_beats.player_text: She gestures to the carriage. 'Simple run. There's a sealed crate in back. You don't open it, you don't lose it, you deliver it to a village in the forest. I'll point you the way and sign you off on delivery. The company pays out when it arrives. Questions?'
player_beats.gm_script: The briefing lays out the job in plain terms. If Sabine is in play, she gives this information; otherwise keep the same facts without making Marlowe the hirer. The crate is the package, never the Keystone Asset. If asked, the briefer can name Hush and the Sablewood preserve.
player_beats.story_takeaway: The contract terms are now explicit and table-facing.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Foreshadow that the journey will ask for rolls once risk appears.
player_beats.player_takeaway: I know the objective, the pay condition, and the don't-open-it rule.

player.title: The package is inspectable but sealed
player.statement: Players can examine the outside without opening it.
player.body: This cue should produce action: who checks the seal, who watches the contact, who positions near the cargo.
player.say: "The crate is visible in the carriage: banded shut, cold at the hinges, and not marked for public handling."
player.ask: If players ask whether they can inspect it: "Yes, the outside. You can look, touch, weigh, smell, or check the seal without opening it."
player.deeper: This cue should produce action: who checks the seal, who watches the contact, who positions near the cargo.

story.title: The crate feels more important than cargo
story.statement: The package hints at wardcraft, mineral wrongness, and official handling.
story.body: Even a success should preserve the reveal. Say wardcraft, stone-like weight, wrong mineral, protective seal; do not say Keystone Asset.
story.say: "It looks like cargo until you pay attention; then it looks like cargo someone paid magic and paperwork to keep quiet."
story.ask: If players ask what an inspection reveals: "Knowledge 14: the seal is contractual and protective. Marlowe Knowledge 13: old, high-tier wardcraft. Varian Instinct 13: wrong-mineral scent under the wax. Khari Strength or Instinct 13: the weight sits low and dense, like stone hidden in freight."
story.deeper: Even a success should preserve the reveal. Say wardcraft, stone-like weight, wrong mineral, protective seal; do not say Keystone Asset.

mechanic.title: Inspection uses approach-based traits
mechanic.statement: The trait depends on how the PC investigates.
mechanic.body: This is a strong teaching moment for Daggerheart traits: the same object can invite different traits based on method.
mechanic.say: "Tell me how you inspect it. Reading the magic is Knowledge. Noticing scent or pressure is Instinct. Testing weight is Strength or Instinct."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for Difficulty: "Use 14 for a general inspection, 13 for a character-specific lane: Marlowe wardcraft, Varian scent, Khari weight-sense."
mechanic.deeper: This is a strong teaching moment for Daggerheart traits: the same object can invite different traits based on method.

player_beats.label: Questions
player_beats.title: What Do You Ask?
player_beats.player_text: She's willing to talk while you load up. What do you want to know?
player_beats.gm_script: Let players interrogate the job. If Sabine is present, use her answers: name if asked; Emeris as employer; Hush as the destination; the forest danger as the company line; sealed means sealed. Marlowe's player also gets bonus insight and an extra Arcana check here.
player_beats.story_takeaway: Players convert unknowns into knowns by asking.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Optional Instinct or Presence 13 can read her nerves; optional Knowledge 14 can sense the official route story is too smooth.
player_beats.player_takeaway: Curiosity pays, and some answers may feel interestingly incomplete.

player.title: Questions move the scene
player.statement: Players can ask direct practical questions before accepting the road.
player.body: Give the table permission to be concrete. This beat is where players learn that curiosity pays.
player.say: "She is willing to talk while the crew loads up. Ask the practical question your character would not leave without asking."
player.ask: If players ask what to ask: "Who are you? Who hired us? Where are we going? What is the route? What happens if the package is damaged? What danger are you not saying plainly?"
player.deeper: Give the table permission to be concrete. This beat is where players learn that curiosity pays.

story.title: The company line has weak spots
story.statement: Answers provide names and practical facts, plus one useful doubt.
story.body: Names are safe here because the players earned them through the briefing. After naming, immediately translate back into plain meaning: company, village, old forest.
story.say: "Her answers are practical: destination, route, pay, and handoff. The uncomfortable part is how rehearsed the safety language sounds."
story.ask: If players ask for names: "Employer: Emeris Crown Holdings. Destination: Hush, a forest village. Route: the old forest road; company maps call it Sablewood."
story.deeper: Names are safe here because the players earned them through the briefing. After naming, immediately translate back into plain meaning: company, village, old forest.

mechanic.title: Question answers can trigger focused rolls
mechanic.statement: Direct questions get direct answers; hidden pressure gets a roll.
mechanic.body: This cue teaches that rolls should add leverage or texture, not block basic information.
mechanic.say: "If you ask a practical question, she answers. If you want to know what is underneath the answer, that is where a roll can happen."
mechanic.ask: If players ask what roll fits: "Knowledge 14 spots the route story as too clean. Instinct or Presence 13 reads her nerves. On Hope, she volunteers one extra practical detail. On Fear, she answers but gets guarded or pushes the crew to leave."
mechanic.deeper: This cue teaches that rolls should add leverage or texture, not block basic information.

player_beats.label: Departure
player_beats.title: You In?
player_beats.player_text: Your contact waits by the carriage. 'We've got a window. You in?' When you're ready, the handoff is signed and the carriage rolls out past the last warded marker and onto the road toward the trees.
player_beats.gm_script: Get a clear yes or boarding moment. If Sabine is in play, this is where her backup job-giver role ends. Either way, the whole crew has received the job together and now owns the route.
player_beats.story_takeaway: The job is accepted and the journey begins.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Commitment and fictional positioning are the mechanic: players choose to board, inspect, ask, or create risk before departure.
player_beats.player_takeaway: We are committed and on the road now.

player.title: The crew commits
player.statement: Players choose to board, position, or force one last action before departure.
player.body: This should close the briefing without hard-cutting player agency.
player.say: "Before the carriage rolls, tell me your last practical move: board, take reins, sit by the crate, ask one final question, or inspect one thing."
player.ask: If players ask whether they can delay: "Yes, briefly. One last question or action, then the job needs to move before the route window closes."
player.deeper: This should close the briefing without hard-cutting player agency.

story.title: The route now belongs to the crew
story.statement: Once they leave, the contact recedes and the party owns the job.
story.body: This prevents the backup contact from becoming a guide NPC. The Prologue hands control to the PCs.
story.say: "The handoff is signed. The contact steps back. The carriage, the package, and the road are yours now."
story.ask: If players ask whether Sabine comes with them: "No. She handles the handoff. The crew takes the route from here."
story.deeper: This prevents the backup contact from becoming a guide NPC. The Prologue hands control to the PCs.

mechanic.title: Commitment and positioning lock in
mechanic.statement: The departure records who drives, who guards the crate, and who watches the road.
mechanic.body: If a PC creates risk before departure, call the roll that matches the action. Tampering with the seal should create employer pressure rather than reveal the contents.
mechanic.say: "Who has the reins, who sits closest to the package, and who is watching the road as you leave?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask why it matters: "Those answers decide who gets the first sensory clue, who can react first to the road, and which trait fits if trouble appears."
mechanic.deeper: If a PC creates risk before departure, call the roll that matches the action. Tampering with the seal should create employer pressure rather than reveal the contents.

player.title: The briefing is playable
player.statement: Players can question the contact, inspect the package, and choose how they leave.
player.body: Keep the scene active. The players should leave knowing they made the job concrete, even if they did not solve the mystery.
player.say: "This is not a cutscene. Ask the contact what you need to know, inspect what you can see, and decide how your character enters the job."
player.ask: If players ask what options matter: "Ask about pay, route, danger, destination, employer, package handling, who drives, where you sit, and whether anyone checks the crate before departure."
player.deeper: Keep the scene active. The players should leave knowing they made the job concrete, even if they did not solve the mystery.

story.title: The job becomes physical
story.statement: Contact, carriage, package, destination, pay, and unease all become visible.
story.body: A direct roleplay read can give the emotional clue. For sharper detail, use Instinct or Presence 13, or Knowledge 14 for the route story.
story.say: "Now the contract has a person, a carriage, a sealed crate, a route, and a deadline."
story.ask: If players ask what feels off: "The contact is too competent to be casual and too nervous to be merely bored. The route story sounds rehearsed."
story.deeper: A direct roleplay read can give the emotional clue. For sharper detail, use Instinct or Presence 13, or Knowledge 14 for the route story.

mechanic.title: Ask, inspect, read, decide
mechanic.statement: The scene teaches the core loop before danger starts.
mechanic.body: This is the first working demonstration of Daggerheart's fiction-first procedure: player intent creates the roll, not a menu of checks.
mechanic.say: "Ask what you ask, inspect what you inspect, and tell me what your character is watching for. I will answer, call for a roll, or hand the spotlight to the next player."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for the likely rolls: "Instinct or Presence 13 reads the contact. Knowledge 14 reads the route story. Marlowe gets a Knowledge 13 wardcraft read on the crate. Varian can use Instinct 13 for scent."
mechanic.deeper: This is the first working demonstration of Daggerheart's fiction-first procedure: player intent creates the roll, not a menu of checks.

story_scope.antagonist_line: Perceived antagonist: the forest. True antagonist: the corporate lie about the forest. The players never confront it directly. They are meant to feel it by the end.
story_scope.gm_thesis: Every act offers at least one guaranteed and one earned hint that the danger is manufactured and the forest is not the enemy.

world_connection_prompts.label: Emeris Crown Holdings
world_connection_prompts.question: You have worked a job like this before. What is the part of the contract you learned to read twice?

title: Entering Sablewood
short: The carriage crosses from city-controlled road into a vast ancient forest and hands off to Act One.
long: A threshold scene. The old forest should land as immense, alive, and older than the company signs nailed into it. Do not linger; the next scene is the road complication.
read: The road narrows between colossal trees. Goldspire waymarkers glow at measured intervals, promising safe passage, customer delight, and limited liability.
gm: Ask one player what comforting lie a corporate sign tells travelers. Use their answer later as irony.
prompt: Horse-drawn carriage carrying five adventurers enters an immense ancient forest road lined with polished glowing Goldspire waymarkers; beautiful but uneasy, no strixwolf yet, no Bramble Union, no undead.
arc_role: Contract orientation, played briefing, and threshold transition
caption: Threshold transition into the ancient forest.
image_alt: Entering Sablewood scene art for Act 0 - The Contract.
image_prompt_used: Horse-drawn carriage carrying five adventurers enters an immense ancient forest road lined with polished glowing Goldspire waymarkers; beautiful but uneasy, no strixwolf yet, no Bramble Union, no undead. Do not include undead, skeletons, wraiths, Open Vale, the Custodian, or the Hanging Office. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: The Old Sable is immense, living, and older than any corporate label. Goldspire has put its waymarkers into the ground, but the forest refuses to feel owned. Run this scene as threshold into branded wilderness and first moral test: The branded wilderness looks managed until the forest begins quietly disagreeing. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: The last warded marker slips behind you. Ahead, the road narrows and the old forest closes around the carriage.
gm_notes: Ask one player what comforting lie a corporate sign tells travelers. Use their answer later as irony.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
sensory_details: painted waymarkers nailed too tightly into living bark
body_language: Barnacle moves where puddles are not
Khari slows when the old trees crowd the road

sample_dialogue.speaker: Varian Soto
sample_dialogue.line: The map calls this controlled habitat. The habitat was not consulted.

public_objective: Cross from the contract briefing into the forest road. The next thing ahead blocks the path.
gm_script: The last warded marker slips behind you. The road narrows, the city noise thins, and the forest rises around the carriage like a green wall. Who has the reins, and what is the first strange detail your character notices about these trees?
player_takeaway: The setting has changed; the forest is now part of the story.
story_takeaway: The party leaves managed civilization for a living place the company only claims to control.

Ask one player what is unique about these trees.

player_beats.label: Threshold
player_beats.title: The Old Forest
player_beats.alt: A carriage enters a colossal green forest road.
player_beats.caption: The road narrows under trees the size of houses.
player_beats.player_text: The last warded marker slides past: a carved stone pillar with brass company stamps bolted to its face. Open country closes into forest. The trees are wrong in scale, trunks wider than the carriage, rising until the canopy swallows the sky. Behind you, the city. Ahead, green light and a long quiet road.
player_beats.gm_script: The trees are bigger than the road was built for. If someone asks what this place is called, say, 'Locals call it the old forest. The company signs call it Sablewood.'
player_beats.story_takeaway: They cross from the safe, branded world into the old forest.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Threshold framing is the mechanic: mark the boundary, ask who has the reins, and let one player author a concrete forest detail.

player.title: The old forest arrives visually
player.statement: Players see scale, green light, and the last managed marker behind them.
player.body: This cue is a sensory handoff from civilization to wild scale.
player.say: "The last warded marker slips behind you. Ahead, trunks wider than the carriage rise until the canopy swallows the sky."
player.ask: If players ask what the marker says: "It is a company road marker bolted over older stone. The new brass wants you to trust the route; the old stone looks like it was here first."
player.deeper: This cue is a sensory handoff from civilization to wild scale.

story.title: Managed safety starts to feel thin
story.statement: The route's official safety markers are newer than the place they mark.
story.body: This plants the corporate-overwrite theme without explaining it.
story.say: "The road is maintained, but the maintenance feels recent. The forest does not."
story.ask: If players inspect the road or signs: "Give the clue plainly: the road is older than the signage nailed beside it."
story.deeper: This plants the corporate-overwrite theme without explaining it.

mechanic.title: Boundary, driver, first-noticer
mechanic.statement: The threshold decides who is physically positioned for the next scene.
mechanic.body: A roll here should foreshadow, not solve. The next slide still carries the first concrete obstacle.
mechanic.say: "Who has the reins as the marker passes behind you, and who is looking out from the carriage?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask what a roll could do: "Instinct 10 can catch that the forest sounds pull away from one direction, foreshadowing the blockage ahead."
mechanic.deeper: A roll here should foreshadow, not solve. The next slide still carries the first concrete obstacle.

player_beats.label: First impressions
player_beats.title: Green Light
player_beats.player_text: From inside the carriage you can hear the forest living around you: low calls in the canopy, croaks in the wet dark, small bodies scattering through underbrush. The light comes down green and filtered. Whatever this place agreed to, it did not agree to be owned.
player_beats.gm_script: You've noticed something unique about the trees here. What is it? And who is driving when the road begins to feel too narrow for the carriage?
player_beats.story_takeaway: The forest is alive and strange, not just a travel lane.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: This reinforces player-authored world detail. Optional Instinct 10 can foreshadow trouble.
player_beats.player_takeaway: I can help build the place with one concrete detail.

player.title: Players can add one forest detail
player.statement: The table helps make the forest vivid with one concrete observation.
player.body: This is a safe creativity prompt: small, sensory, optional, and bounded.
player.say: "Give me one concrete detail your character notices: sound, smell, light, motion, temperature, or something about the trees."
player.ask: If a player freezes: "You can take one of mine: green light, wet bark smell, animal calls above you, roots like old hands, or a road too narrow for comfort."
player.deeper: This is a safe creativity prompt: small, sensory, optional, and bounded.

story.title: The forest is alive, not scenery
story.statement: The place reacts through sound, scale, and quiet.
story.body: Use per-character hooks to distribute attention without making every moment a roll.
story.say: "The forest is not a backdrop. It has weather, breath, animals, and old paths under the company road."
story.ask: If players ask what their PC senses: "Varian catches layered smells first; Barnacle notices what would make a good hiding place; Garrick reads the road like security exposure; Khari feels how small the carriage is under the trees; Marlowe notices wardcraft fading behind them."
story.deeper: Use per-character hooks to distribute attention without making every moment a roll.

mechanic.title: Sensory spotlight can become Instinct
mechanic.statement: Free description becomes an Instinct roll only when the player pushes for warning.
mechanic.body: On Fear, still give the warning but make it late, partial, or unnerving.
mechanic.say: "A sensory detail is free. If you are trying to read danger from it, roll Instinct."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for Difficulty: "Instinct 10 gives a broad warning that sound thins near the bend. Varian gets the clearest direction on success because scent and hearing are their lane."
mechanic.deeper: On Fear, still give the warning but make it late, partial, or unnerving.

player_beats.label: Hand-off
player_beats.title: Something Blocks The Path
player_beats.player_text: The road bends ahead, tight around a stand of trees. Your driver eases the carriage into the curve, and something is blocking the path.
player_beats.gm_script: The road bends tight around a stand of ancient trunks. As the carriage comes through the curve, something is blocking the path.
player_beats.story_takeaway: The quiet road delivers its first complication.
player_beats.mechanic_takeaway: Next scene brings the first action pressure.

player.title: The first obstacle is about to enter
player.statement: Players understand the quiet road is becoming active play.
player.body: This cue is the handoff, not the whole encounter. It should create forward pull.
player.say: "The carriage eases around the bend, and something is blocking the path."
player.ask: If players ask what they see: "Hold that for the next scene: shapes on the road, the carriage slowing, and enough time for one immediate reaction."
player.deeper: This cue is the handoff, not the whole encounter. It should create forward pull.

story.title: The route complication arrives
story.statement: The delivery is no longer only a contract; the road now pushes back.
story.body: Keep identity withheld until the Act One scene starts. Description first, proper nouns later.
story.say: "Whatever the company promised, the road has its own first answer."
story.ask: If players ask whether this is an ambush: "Your characters do not know yet. You know the path is blocked and the carriage is losing easy forward motion."
story.deeper: Keep identity withheld until the Act One scene starts. Description first, proper nouns later.

mechanic.title: Cut on pressure
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is pacing: end the Prologue on the first actionable pressure.
mechanic.body: This protects pacing and prevents the threshold from absorbing the Act One encounter.
mechanic.say: "Pause there. That is our handoff into the first road problem."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for an immediate reaction: "You can call out, grab the reins, move toward the package, or look ahead. The next scene will resolve what that means."
mechanic.deeper: This protects pacing and prevents the threshold from absorbing the Act One encounter.

player.title: The table crosses a threshold
player.statement: Players know the setting has changed and the forest matters.
player.body: This transition should be brief, sensory, and playable. It is not a second lore briefing.
player.say: "The city falls behind. The road narrows. The old forest becomes the room around the carriage."
player.ask: If players ask what to do here: "Tell me who has the reins, where your character is in the carriage, and one thing they notice as the trees close in."
player.deeper: This transition should be brief, sensory, and playable. It is not a second lore briefing.

story.title: The company does not own the old forest
story.statement: The forest feels older and larger than the signs claiming it.
story.body: Use size and sensory language first: trunks wider than a carriage, green filtered light, animal calls dropping quiet, brass signs bolted to older stone.
story.say: "The signs say the route is managed. The trees make that claim feel very small."
story.ask: If players ask what the forest is called: "Locals call it the old forest. The company signs call it Sablewood."
story.deeper: Use size and sensory language first: trunks wider than a carriage, green filtered light, animal calls dropping quiet, brass signs bolted to older stone.

mechanic.title: Threshold framing hands players authorship
mechanic.statement: Ask who drives and let one player add a concrete forest detail.
mechanic.body: This reinforces that players can author sensory details when invited, while Kyle keeps control of hidden causes and the next obstacle.
mechanic.say: "Before the road problem appears, who has the reins, and what is one strange detail your character notices about these trees?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask for a roll: "Most details are free. Use Instinct 10 if someone wants a hint of trouble before the next scene; success points toward where the forest goes quiet."
mechanic.deeper: This reinforces that players can author sensory details when invited, while Kyle keeps control of hidden causes and the next obstacle.

story_scope.antagonist_line: Perceived antagonist: the forest. True antagonist: the corporate lie about the forest. The players never confront it directly. They are meant to feel it by the end.
story_scope.gm_thesis: Every act offers at least one guaranteed and one earned hint that the danger is manufactured and the forest is not the enemy.

A player asking what they know receives the corporate line: strixwolves are vicious pack predators.

title: The Overturned Vendor Cart
short: The party finds a vendor cart blocking the road, with spilled produce, invoices, and a useless incident placard.
long: This is the first crack in the official story. The route promised safety, but the cart is ruined, the driver is dead, and the system’s response is decorative.
read: A vendor cart lies sideways across the road. Produce and invoices spill into the mud. A polished placard blinks: INCIDENT RESPONSE EXPECTED WITHIN 3–5 BUSINESS DAYS.
gm: The placard can be a standard route-monitoring glyph, not proof that anyone meaningfully knows what happened.
prompt: Overturned vendor cart blocks branded forest logistics road; scattered produce, invoices, broken wheel, polished incident placard; adventurers arrive cautiously; no strixwolf in center, maybe only a shadow nearby; no undead.
arc_role: Threshold into branded wilderness and first moral test
caption: The overturned cart gives the party a mystery before it gives them a fight.
image_alt: The Overturned Vendor Cart scene art for The Logistics Incident.
image_prompt_used: Overturned vendor cart blocks branded forest logistics road; scattered produce, invoices, broken wheel, polished incident placard; adventurers arrive cautiously; no strixwolf in center, maybe only a shadow nearby; no undead. Do not include undead, skeletons, wraiths, Open Vale, the Custodian, or the Hanging Office. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: This is the first crack in the official story. The route promised safety, but the cart is ruined, the driver is dead, and the system’s response is decorative. Run this scene as threshold into branded wilderness and first moral test: The overturned cart gives the party a mystery before it gives them a fight. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: A vendor cart lies sideways across the road. Produce and invoices spill into the mud. A polished placard blinks: INCIDENT RESPONSE EXPECTED WITHIN 3–5 BUSINESS DAYS.
gm_notes: The placard can be a standard route-monitoring glyph, not proof that anyone meaningfully knows what happened.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Sablewood route lore: this is an approved path, and the body/cart disruption should feel like a coverage failure as much as a wilderness event.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
[KEEP/EARNED] The driver died from a cut throat; the strixwolf did not kill him. (Instinct or Knowledge Medium 15)
[ADD/EARNED] Near the cart is a pre-written Grail "Hazard Confirmed: Strixwolf Attack" tag. (Finesse or Instinct Medium 15)
sensory_details: blood under wheel-ruts instead of claw marks
Sunken road walls press close enough to feel like a product corridor carved through something ancient.
body_language: Marlowe steps between the crate and the wreck
Garrick kneels before touching anything
Barnacle scans for whoever benefits

Keystone Asset™: Inside the sealed crate, packed in wax-paper and reassurance, sits a heavy grey stone the size of a loaf, warm to the touch, faintly humming, with a light deep inside it that is slowly going out.

Incident Response Placard™: A flat brass disc on a post holds a watchful glyph and a single cheerful bell. When trouble happens nearby, the glyph lights, the bell rings once, brightly, and then nothing else happens at all.

Sableblade: Growing straight up out of dark forest soil, like a sapling that decided to be a sword, is a blade of living dark wood and pale metal. It has no maker's mark and hums when your hand nears the hilt.
Recall Stone: A smooth grey pebble feels warm and ordinary until it refuses to stay where you put it. Set it down, look away, and it waits back in your palm.
Goldwater Liability Token™: A heavy brass chit with a smiling coin-face drops into your palm like a tiny verdict. The fine print is too small to read without feeling blamed.
Tamsin's Home-Token: A small thumb-polished token on a cord hangs beside the torn blue scarf, warm from wear and etched with a tiny house mark instead of a company seal.
Cracked Pocket Ward™: A cheap little ward charm sits cracked down the middle, still trying to glow through a smiling warranty sticker.

title: The Fallout Investigation
short: The party discovers clues that the strixwolf was not the whole story.
long: The dead driver’s neck was slit. The cart was stripped. Bramble and old shipping seals suggest deliberate interference with the route.
read: The wreck tells a second story. Some damage is animal hunger. Some is not.
gm: Give clues generously. The goal is not to hide the ambush forever; the goal is to let players feel clever before the trap springs.

world_connection_prompts.label: The Bramble Union
world_connection_prompts.question: You have been desperate enough to do something you are not proud of. What was it, and would you do it again to eat?

title: Bramble Union Ambush
short: Bramble Union reclaimers attack the carriage to seize the cargo.
long: The Bramble Union are the immediate antagonists, but they are desperate rather than cartoon evil. They are dangerous, armed, and under pressure.
read: Bramblefolk burst from the undergrowth, blades drawn. Their eyes keep flicking toward the carriage. They are here for the cargo.
gm: Offer ways to incapacitate, scare off, capture, or negotiate if players push for it.
prompt: Dynamic forest ambush: bramblefolk reclaimers spring from thorny brush to seize carriage cargo; armor patched with stones, shipping seals, torn contract tags; adventurers defend carriage; no strixwolf, no undead.
arc_role: External opposition and morally complicated conflict
caption: The Bramble Union ambush should feel dangerous and understandable at the same time.
image_alt: Bramble Union Ambush scene art for Cargo Reclaimers.
image_prompt_used: Dynamic forest ambush: bramblefolk reclaimers spring from thorny brush to seize carriage cargo; armor patched with stones, shipping seals, torn contract tags; adventurers defend carriage; no strixwolf, no undead. Do not include the Strixwolf Mother, strixwolf pups, wolves, owlbears, or animal companions unless explicitly requested. Do not include undead, skeletons, wraiths, Open Vale, the Custodian, or the Hanging Office. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: The Bramble Union are the immediate antagonists, but they are desperate rather than cartoon evil. They are dangerous, armed, and under pressure. Run this scene as external opposition and morally complicated conflict: The Bramble Union ambush should feel dangerous and understandable at the same time. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: Bramblefolk burst from the undergrowth, blades drawn. Their eyes keep flicking toward the carriage. They are here for the cargo.
gm_notes: Offer ways to incapacitate, scare off, capture, or negotiate if players push for it.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
The Bramble Union ambush now points back to hidden villages, stoneweave armor, and thorns used as shelter from surveillance.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
[REFLAVOR/GUARANTEED] The reclaimers target the cargo and manifest, not purses, and avoid killing when possible.
[REFLAVOR/GUARANTEED] Their gear includes salvaged, repainted Grail/Kazrak kit: ex-workers, not feral bandits. (Knowledge Medium 15 to name the issue)
[ADD/EARNED] "That stone belongs in the ground." "You do not know what you are carrying."
sensory_details: a shout that sounds rehearsed because fear needed a script
body_language: The Claimrunner looks at the crate more than the party
Ambushers hesitate when civilians are named

sample_dialogue.line: That box buys another month of their safety and another year of ours getting sold.

sample_dialogue.line: You do not get to solve theft with a corpse in the road.

loot: Use Bramble Union Ambushers and Claimrunner loot tables
Bramble Union Stoneweave: A garment of thousands of tiny polished stones moves like cloth and turns thorns like armor. Every fitted piece looks cut by hands that loved the work.
Vial of Briarpowder: A small stoppered vial holds fine grey-green thorn powder that seems to drink the light. A blade edge near it looks sharper and hungrier.
Bramble Ward-Scrap Charm Cluster: A knot of blue ward shards, twine, and tiny salvage tags clacks softly at a Bramblefolk belt. It looks illegal only because it looks useful.

Claimrunner Serrated Blade: A short serrated blade shows careful filing along the back edge and a handle wrapped in road cord. It is ugly in the practical way of a tool that has never had a decorative day.

loot: Personal effects
Route sketch
Old Goldspire seal
Bramble Union Stoneweave: A garment of thousands of tiny polished stones moves like cloth and turns thorns like armor. Every fitted piece looks cut by hands that loved the work.
Vial of Briarpowder: A small stoppered vial holds fine grey-green thorn powder that seems to drink the light. A blade edge near it looks sharper and hungrier.
Bramble Ward-Scrap Charm Cluster: A knot of blue ward shards, twine, and tiny salvage tags clacks softly at a Bramblefolk belt. It looks illegal only because it looks useful.

Claimrunner Serrated Blade: A short serrated blade shows careful filing along the back edge and a handle wrapped in road cord. It is ugly in the practical way of a tool that has never had a decorative day.

title: Arrival at Hush
short: The party enters Hush, a real warm village inside corporate branding.
long: The tone shifts from danger to welcome. Hush is officially a Community Enclave, but locally it is home.
read: You pass the ward pillar and feel a small pop, like a bubble closing behind you. The forest quiets. Friendly voices rise ahead.
gm: Do not make Hush the joke. The branding is the joke; the people are sincere.

title: The Clover Co-op
short: The party visits the Clover Co-op, the social heart of Hush.
long: This is where the village becomes lovable. Shoes on the line, polished gifts, music, food, and local ritual should make the players want to save this place.
read: The Clover Co-op climbs six stories up an ancient tree. The room smells of bread, moss tea, old wood, and somebody’s terrible but enthusiastic fiddle.
gm: Let players invent one cozy custom. Fold it into the epilogue.

short: The road to the Custodian passes through mosslit farms and carved watching trees.
long: The scene drifts from cozy village into older magic. The land is alive and watching.
read: Blue moss glows over the crops like starlight caught in soil. The trees ahead have faces carved into every side.
gm: This is a good place to ask Khari’s old name for Sablewood if it has not come up.

title: The Keystone Reveal
short: The crate contains the Keystone Asset / ward-stone tied to major protective infrastructure.
long: This is the turn. The job was never ordinary. The corporation concealed a ward failure because public knowledge would invite panic, predators, and acquisition.
read: Inside the sealed crate is a massive stone with a lion’s face carved into it. The room goes quiet before anyone speaks.
gm: This is where Marlowe realizes how much was withheld from her too, unless you want her to know already.
prompt: Interior of cluttered magical maintenance office; Custodian opens sealed crate with glowing ward-stone carved with lion face; adventurers realize job is bigger; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no undead.
caption: The Keystone Asset stops being cargo and becomes a communal protection problem.
image_alt: The Keystone Reveal scene art for The Hanging Office.
image_prompt_used: Interior of cluttered magical maintenance office; Custodian opens sealed crate with glowing ward-stone carved with lion face; adventurers realize job is bigger; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no undead. Do not include the Strixwolf Mother, strixwolf pups, wolves, owlbears, or animal companions unless explicitly requested. No strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no undead. Focus on the Custodian and the Keystone Asset reveal. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: This is the turn. The job was never ordinary. The corporation concealed a ward failure because public knowledge would invite panic, predators, and acquisition. Run this scene as mentor-custodian truth reveal: The Keystone Asset stops being cargo and becomes a communal protection problem. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: Inside the sealed crate is a massive stone with a lion’s face carved into it. The room goes quiet before anyone speaks.
gm_notes: This is where Marlowe realizes how much was withheld from her too, unless you want her to know already.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
[KEEP/GUARANTEED] The sealed package is the capital's ward Keystone; the city is unwarded while it is away.
[ADD/SEED] "Your capital's safety is older than your contracts. It is the very thing they teach you to fear."
[ADD/EARNED] The Keystone's magic is pre-corporate forest-ward work, the same school companies call primitive. (Knowledge Hard 20)
sensory_details: a low tone felt in teeth
body_language: Marlowe looks guilty before she looks relieved
The Custodian touches the crate like an apology

title: Short Rest Before the Storm
short: The party takes a short rest while the Custodian prepares the ritual.
long: This is the breath before the ordeal. Let characters tend wounds, prepare, or share one quiet line.
read: For a little while, the Old Sable gives you room to breathe.
gm: Ask each player how they prepare. Give them ownership of the battlefield.
prompt: Adventurers resting around ritual clearing: repairing armor, tending wounds, checking weapons, while Custodian prepares runes around Keystone Asset; ominous calm; no monsters yet.
caption: The short rest is a pressure valve, not dead air.
image_alt: Short Rest Before the Storm scene art for The Ward Renewal.
image_prompt_used: Adventurers resting around ritual clearing: repairing armor, tending wounds, checking weapons, while Custodian prepares runes around Keystone Asset; ominous calm; no monsters yet. Do not include the Strixwolf Mother, strixwolf pups, wolves, owlbears, or animal companions unless explicitly requested. No Strixwolf. No Bramble Union. Only Legacy Security Skeletons and Soul-Audit Wraiths as threats. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: This is the breath before the ordeal. Let characters tend wounds, prepare, or share one quiet line. Run this scene as ordeal, ritual defense, and restoration: The short rest is a pressure valve, not dead air. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: For a little while, the Old Sable gives you room to breathe.
gm_notes: Ask each player how they prepare. Give them ownership of the battlefield.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
sensory_details: the Keystone ticking like a second pulse
body_language: Players can show care through small prep
The Custodian only sits if invited

title: Legacy Security Skeletons
short: Old ward-security remnants rise with rusted swords.
long: They are not random undead. They are obsolete security protocols made bone and rust.
read: Four skeletons tear upward from the soil, rusted swords raised like policies nobody remembered to cancel.
gm: Use them to teach group attacks and countdown progress.
prompt: Rusted skeleton warriors claw up from ritual clearing, old security sigils hanging from bones; party braces around Custodian and Keystone Asset; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union.
caption: Legacy Security Skeletons are old protection logic with the people scraped out.
image_alt: Legacy Security Skeletons scene art for The Ward Renewal.
image_prompt_used: Rusted skeleton warriors claw up from ritual clearing, old security sigils hanging from bones; party braces around Custodian and Keystone Asset; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union. Do not include the Strixwolf Mother, strixwolf pups, wolves, owlbears, or animal companions unless explicitly requested. No Strixwolf. No Bramble Union. Only Legacy Security Skeletons and Soul-Audit Wraiths as threats. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: They are not random undead. They are obsolete security protocols made bone and rust. Run this scene as ordeal, ritual defense, and restoration: Legacy Security Skeletons are old protection logic with the people scraped out. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.

title: The Relay Spire Hook
short: The Custodian reveals another relay spire may be failing.
long: This closes the one-shot and opens the campaign door. The system’s failure was not isolated.
read: “It’s good to have heroes in the Old Sable again.”
gm: End here. Do not over-explain the next adventure unless players ask.
prompt: Cinematic pullback above Sablewood: stone relay spires break through treeline with small flames, one distant spire burns thin; party looks toward horizon from Hanging Office; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no undead foreground.
caption: The Relay Spire hook points beyond the one-shot without stealing this ending.
image_alt: The Relay Spire Hook scene art for Beyond the Contract.
image_prompt_used: Cinematic pullback above Sablewood: stone relay spires break through treeline with small flames, one distant spire burns thin; party looks toward horizon from Hanging Office; no strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no undead foreground. Do not include the Strixwolf Mother, strixwolf pups, wolves, owlbears, or animal companions unless explicitly requested. No strixwolf, no Bramble Union, no skeletons, no wraiths, no combat unless explicitly requested. 4:3 cinematic fantasy concept art, no visible text, no captions, no logos, no UI, no watermark.
long_storyboard: This closes the one-shot and opens the campaign door. The system’s failure was not isolated. Run this scene as return, consequence, and next hook: The Relay Spire hook points beyond the one-shot without stealing this ending. Keep the camera close to practical choices, visible consequences, and the difference between ordinary people and the infrastructure pressing on them.
read_aloud: “It’s good to have heroes in the Old Sable again.”
gm_notes: End here. Do not over-explain the next adventure unless players ask.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
[KEEP/GUARANTEED] A nearby Relay Spire beacon burns weakly, pointing to the larger thread.
sensory_details: ward chimes answering out of sync
body_language: The Custodian watches the distance before saying anything
Marlowe does not pretend she failed to hear

official_results.critical_success: Critical Success: best possible version of the action; gain Hope and clear 1 Stress. Add an extra benefit that follows from the fiction.
official_results.success_with_hope: Success with Hope: the PC gets what they wanted and gains Hope. Keep the position clean or generous.
official_results.success_with_fear: Success with Fear: the PC gets what they wanted, but the GM gains Fear and introduces a cost, complication, or pressure.
official_results.failure_with_hope: Failure with Hope: the PC does not get the full result, but gains Hope and receives a useful thread, clue, or safer next option.
official_results.failure_with_fear: Failure with Fear: the PC fails and the GM gains Fear. Make a hard move that follows from the fiction.

outcomes.hard_failure: The wrong report protects the stack more than Hush. Use a hard complication, lost time, worse position, GM Fear, or mark Stress. Apply an official condition only if the fiction and rules justify it.
outcomes.near_miss: The attempt falls short, but a partial thread appears. Offer one clue, weak position, or safer follow-up.
outcomes.mixed_success: The PC gets the core result, but it costs time, noise, leverage, or a visible resource.
